content.intro: This lesson focuses on json in javascript and connects the PDF syllabus topics to a small, inspectable example. Work from the intended data model, write down the expected result, then verify syntax and semantics with the target tool.
content.why_it_matters: JSON in JavaScript matters because structured-data files sit between people, tools, services, and deployment systems. A clear contract and repeatable checks make the result easier to maintain and safer to consume.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: JSON is a common representation for HTTP payloads and application boundaries. Reliable APIs define stable resource shapes, validate input, report errors consistently, version contracts carefully, and avoid confusing transport status with payload content.

content_blocks.title: What you will cover
content_blocks.text: This lesson explicitly addresses: JSON text versus JavaScript values. JSON.parse(). JSON.stringify(). Parsing errors. Revivers and replacers.; Serialization limitations. Avoiding confusion between parsing and evaluating source code.. Treat each as part of a workflow: define what the data should mean, represent it consistently, and test how the chosen implementation interprets it.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: JSON in JavaScript
content_blocks.expected_output: With a JavaScript runtime, JSON.parse turns text into a value and JSON.stringify serializes a value back to text.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run with a local JavaScript runtime, or inspect the snippet statically. The browser playground only runs browser-supported HTML/CSS/JavaScript and the required Node-only APIs may not exist in the browser.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the starting fixture before each test. Change one field, indentation level, parser option, or schema constraint at a time, then compare the result with the prediction.
content_blocks.limitations: This snippet is a reference/example, not evidence that the CodeLeaf browser executes JSON/YAML parsing, shell commands, or Python. Validate locally with a named parser or tool before relying on it.

content_blocks.text: Validate syntax first, then check the intended types and meaning. A document that parses can still violate the data contract or business rules. Confirm implementation-specific behavior against the target parser, tool version, and standards documentation.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating readable text as proof of correctness.
common_mistakes.why: Syntax and visual formatting cannot establish data types, schema conformance, or application-specific meaning.
common_mistakes.fix: Parse, validate against the intended contract, and test a valid plus an invalid fixture.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming every parser interprets the feature identically.
common_mistakes.why: Format versions, schema choices, library defaults, and product-specific restrictions affect behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Record the exact parser/version and test the target environment.

common_mistakes.why: Missing fields, wrong types, duplicate keys, or ambiguous scalars may still break consumers.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep valid, invalid, and boundary fixtures in version control.
